title: LedgerCore resilience and fallback orchestration review
summary: Follow-up on the June 9th production degradation: review of root cause analysis, proposed mitigations (KV cache fencing, graceful fallback to smaller model variants), verification plan for canary, and security/audit implications for log retention. Agreed owner list and next steps for a resilience pilot next week.
next_steps: Jordan to run targeted KV corruption sim and upload logs to shared folder by 2027-06-22
Elena to validate RBAC change with infra team and confirm approval by 2027-06-21
Maya to share dedicated pricing + pilot SOW by 2027-06-18
All: schedule 30-min canary run review on 2027-06-24
action_items: Jordan: simulate KV cache corruption and produce a short reproducible script + logs (due 2027-06-22)
Elena: coordinate infra window and RBAC approval, confirm if KMS rotation policy impacts logging (due 2027-06-21)
Maya: send updated SOW/pilot pricing and reference checklist (due 2027-06-18)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-15 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 61m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (LedgerCore), Elena Voss (LedgerCore SRE), Tomás Ruiz (LedgerCore InfoSec)

Summary: quick follow-up on last week's incident, dig into KV-cache edge case, plan canary and fallbacks, check audit/logging implications for compliance.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll run about an hour, we've added Jordan from SE to go into the KV details, I'll kick things off with the RCA highlights.
[00:28] Samir: thanks maya. quick context — the outages on the 9th are high impact for us, so we need concrete mitigations and a clear test plan.
[00:45] Jordan: yeah, hi. so short version from our RCA: there was a rare sequence of prefix evictions in the K-V cache under a burst pattern, that coupled with a routing fallback misconfiguration led to a cold-start storm on the larger model variant. we saw queue depth increase and some nodes hit ephemeral OOMs, which triggered autoscaler churn.
[01:20] Elena: when you say prefix evictions — are those periodic TTLs or eviction from memory pressure? sometimes our infra masks memory pressure as eviction, hard to tell.
[01:38] Jordan: good question, it's primarily memory pressure + a GC-ish cleanup path in our K-V layer that didn't respect the fencing per tenant. so tenant A's eviction batched and mistakenly reclaimed some chunk used by tenant B during a race. the logs show shared pointers being nulled, um that is, the pointers were cleared early.
[02:07] Tomás: that sounds like cross-tenant data safety but I thought you had logical isolation for KV?
[02:15] Jordan: we do but there was a lower-level pooling optimization to reduce allocations; it introduced a reuse pattern that didn't fully tag buffers with tenant id on one fast path. its rare but triggered under the particular sequence.
[02:34] Samir: ok so how do we prevent?
[02:36] Jordan: short-term — we can enable KV fencing (disallow reuse on that path) and increase conservative cache thresholds + turn on aggressive prefix spill-to-disk for high-burst routes. Also enforce a rate-limiter on the route that landed the large-model Fall back.
[02:58] Maya: to be clear we have two mitigation buckets: software patch to the K-V reuse path, and operational controls (routing policy change + rate limits + smaller model default). we'll outline a canary to validate.
[03:18] Elena: the patch — is that risky for latency? our SLAs are tight. If we fence we might increase per-token latency.
[03:29] Jordan: yes small increase in p99, about 6-12ms in our bench for small sequences; we can offset by switching that workload to continuous-batching. there is a tradeoff, but it's predictable versus the risk of corruption.
[03:50] Samir: I'd rather accept small p99 bump than another outage.
[03:53] Tomás: also we need to check audit trail — the incident had partial logs missing for the period of the spike, InfoSec will want a record. what retention are you using?
[04:06] Maya: by default hosted uses 30 days, enterprise can configure up to 1 year. we can provide an extended retention add-on for the pilot and also export to your SIEM.
[04:19] Tomás: export format? we run an internal splunk cluster — examples would help.
[04:24] Jordan: we'll share a sample export (json-lines) and the mapping for fields used in the latency and model-reroute traces. we'll link to a repo.
[04:36] Elena: note — rotation of our KMS keys is monthly; if logs are encrypted customer-side we need to ensure Redwood supports keys that rotate with our schedule.
[04:48] Maya: yes we support BYOK with rotation. we'll include the KMS notes in the security doc.
[05:01] 
[05:10] Jordan: proposed canary plan: 1) enable KV fencing in a blue env, 2) run a synthetic burst workload that replicates the July 9th traffic shape (we have the traces), 3) compare model routing under load with fallback enabled, 4) validate that no cross-tenant memory reclamation occurs and no autoscaler thrash for 2h.
[05:38] Samir: timeline?
[05:40] Jordan: we can produce the canary script by EOD tomorrow, need a 2-hour infra window next week.
[05:46] Maya: ledgercore prefers windows Wed mornings, Elena?
[05:50] Elena: wed morning works, but I'll confirm with infra and the change advisory board.
[05:55] Tomás: and we'll need an audit packet for compliance judges — can we get a pre-run brief?
[06:01] Maya: yes we'll do a pre-run brief doc and share checklist.
[06:06] 
[06:15] Samir: curious — you mentioned fallback to smaller model. can you explain the logic there and the routing policy? we've seen quality drop a lot when fallback triggers.
[06:26] Jordan: absolutely. current policy uses latency-first fallback: when the large-model queue exceeds threshold X, route to medium-model variant that's quantized. we include a scoring penalty in the routing decision to avoid quality regressions; the idea is to prefer degraded but correct outputs instead of failures. we also can route only on a per-customer token budget instead of global queue to avoid cross-tenant impact.
[06:55] Elena: per-customer threshold makes sense. we also want to log when fallback happens with exact prompt snippet hash for later eval.
[07:06] Jordan: agreed, we'll attach a prompt-hash and confidence bucket. privacy note: the prompt-hash is one-way, not able to reconstruct.
[07:15] Tomás: fine but include the legal team — certain regulated prompts we may want to never fallback. can we add a denylist?
[07:23] Maya: yes, per-customer denylist and a per-route flag. we'll include that in the policy doc.
[07:30] 
[07:35] Samir: last time the autoscaler churned because the fallback triggered many long-lived sessions to start new model containers. how do we avoid a cold-start cascade?
[07:46] Jordan: two levers: warm standby pools for the fallback models (dedicated small pool) and a soft-start for containers (pre-warm lightweight LRU containers). Redwood Dedicated customers can choose reserved capacity; for hosted we provide a small guaranteed pool for critical routes.
[08:05] Samir: ok pricing aside, we need a reliability guarantee in the SOW.
[08:09] Maya: we'll add objective metrics for p95/p99 and fallback rate thresholds to the pilot SOW.
[08:15] 
[08:20] Elena: about logs — during the incident some traces were sampled out. can we increase sampling temporarily for the canary run?
[08:28] Jordan: yes we can bump tracing to 100% for a window and dump KV internals. note that increases traffic to the logging pipeline; we'll coordinate retention.
[08:38] Tomás: that will have storage implications — do you support on-prem log ingestion?
[08:42] Maya: yes we can push logs to your S3 or via syslog to your cluster. we'll share examples.
[08:49] 
[09:00] Jordan: quick note on verification: our test harness will validate three invariants every 10s: no buffer reuse cross-tenant, queue depth stays below threshold, and model route latencies within expected bands. we'll produce a daily digest after the canary.
[09:19] Samir: good. one more ask: can you simulate a network partition during the canary? last outage had a coincident network blip which exacerbated thrash.
[09:30] Jordan: yes we can introduce packet loss and increased latency in the burst script; we'll label that scenario "partition-plus-burst".
[09:37] 
[09:40] Maya: ok let's capture owners and due dates. Jordan will produce KV sim and the canary harness by 2027-06-22; Elena will confirm infra window and RBAC by 2027-06-21; Tomás will send compliance questions by 2027-06-20; Maya will send SOW and pricing by 2027-06-18.
[10:03] Samir: that works. We'll plan the review for June 24th.
[10:08] 
[10:12] Tomás: small security question — during the incident our SIEM showed a gap between trace IDs and some tokens. do you maintain a mapping?
[10:21] Jordan: we retain trace->request mapping for 30 days by default; we can extend or ship to your SIEM. mapping is hashed.
[10:32] Tomás: please provide sample hashes and mapping cadence so we can align.
[10:36] Jordan: will do.
[10:39] 
[10:45] Elena: also, we discovered one of our routes was misrouted to a general-purpose queue instead of the low-latency path. is there a way to pin routes to the low-latency pool?
[10:55] Maya: yes there's a route-level pool binding you can set in the Console or via API. Jordan can show the policy snippet.
[11:05] Jordan: I'll paste policy examples and a terraform snippet to bind the route.
[11:12] 
[11:20] Samir: Great. Any blockers?
[11:23] Elena: none from SRE aside from infra confirmation.
[11:26] Tomás: none from InfoSec as long as we get the audit packet.
[11:29] Maya: perfect. recap — action items as we discussed, canary week window Wed, June 23-25 proposed, follow-up review on June 24th 15:00 UTC.
[11:45] Samir: thanks everyone.
[11:47] Maya: thanks, we'll share the notes and links to the simulator + canary checklist.
[11:52]
